The reform that returned farming in China from collective communes to individual families, starting in 1978 and made national by 1982. The land stayed publicly owned, but each household leased plots, delivered a set quota of grain to the state and kept or sold the rest.

It started from below. In late 1978, eighteen farmers in the poor village of Xiaogang, in Anhui, secretly agreed to divide the commune land among their families. They signed a pact with their thumbprints, promising to raise each other's children if the leaders were jailed. Their harvest the next year was far bigger than before. Provincial leaders protected them, and Deng Xiaoping backed the idea as part of reform and opening.

Why it worked:

  • Under the people's communes, work points paid the same whether people worked hard or not. Now families kept what they grew.
  • Farmers chose what to plant and sold the surplus in reopened markets.
  • Grain output rose sharply in the early 1980s, ending the hunger that had haunted China since the Great Chinese Famine.

Freed from the fields, tens of millions of farmers moved into rural industry and later into the cities, despite the limits of the hukou household registration. The contract in Xiaogang is now displayed in a national museum, and the village is a site of pilgrimage for the reform era.
